confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_quote: 2.3.2 Stress. Stress does not appear to be phonemic. It most often occurs on the penultimate syllable, but there are exceptions. As with tone, more work needs to be done in this area.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote: confirmed verbatim at Siegel 1984:89 sec. 2.3.2 in the PDF we hold (p.7 = printed p.89); the record's own quote/cite/loc fields are blank because the record is an StressTyp2 coding, with the verified quotation stored under sources/the domain quotation. (2) Deciding source: a 1984 Pacific Linguistics grammar sketch, self-described as preliminary, whose whole stress treatment is two hedged sentences; it is nonetheless the only description of Labu that exists (Glottolog: one descriptive work; Holzknecht 1989 silent on stress; SIL OPD 2004 derivative of Siegel; no sketch in Lynch, Ross & Crowley 2002; no instrumental/phonology paper found), so we hold the best available source. (3) list of works to obtain is short and low-priority: Holzknecht 1994 (paywalled de Gruyter chapter) is the only unread Labu-specific work and is a contact/change study, not a phonology. (4) Status 'thin' rather than 'well-source

sources.quote: "Stress does not appear to be phonemic. It most often occurs on the penultimate syllable, but there are exceptions. Tone (or pitch) is phonemically significant. ... could be described as a register tone language." — a verbatim restatement of Siegel 1984:89; bibliography lists only Siegel 1984, so it is derivative, not independent.
sources.note: Cited by Wikipedia as a Labu phonology source; downloaded now via the Internet Archive — its suprasegmentals paragraph copies Siegel 1984:89, so it adds a second attestation but no independent evidence.

sources.quote: None. Section gives the phoneme inventory, syllable notes ('All word final syllables in Labu are open') and note 7: 'Tonal contrasts are phonemic in Labu ... (see Siegel, 1984:88-89 for minimal pairs) ... Tone is not predictable in Labu as it is in Yabem and Bukawa'. The only 'stress' hits in the volume concern folk perceptions of dialect difference and Duwet/Watut vowel reduction, not Labu.
